argument: Jürgen Habermas defends the Enlightenment against critics like Adorno and Horkheimer, arguing that its failures were not proof the project was doomed but evidence it was incomplete. Adorno and Horkheimer only recognized two kinds of reason -- statements about the world and 'instrumental reason' (means-to-an-end thinking) -- and missed a third: 'communicative rationality,' the reason embedded in genuine conversation between people who share values and actually believe what they say. This third type of reason is what built the 'public sphere' (coffee houses, salons, newspapers) and underlies real democracy. But over time 'the system' -- the fused economic-governmental machine run on instrumental reason -- has increasingly colonized the 'life world' where communicative rationality happens, most visibly through media that now sells us values the way a salesman sells a phone case. True democracy, to Habermas, means reversing that: the life world controlling the system, not the other way around.
keyIdeas: Habermas thinks Adorno and Horkheimer's critique of Enlightenment reason was flawed because they defined reason too narrowly, recognizing only instrumental reason and statements about the world, while ignoring communicative rationality.

Instrumental reason (illustrated by the fork-and-buffalo example) lets you rationally plan a sequence of steps toward a goal even when the goal itself is absurd -- rationality alone can't tell you what the goal should be.

A successful act of communication must be intelligible, treated as a legitimate topic, sincerely believed by the speaker, and reasoned within values both parties share -- this is 'communicative rationality,' distinct from 'strategic rationality' (like a salesman who doesn't believe his own pitch).

The 'public sphere' emerged from mass print combined with coffee houses and salons in early-Enlightenment Europe, letting the rising middle class read the news and debate it -- something the illiterate, disenfranchised peasantry of feudal France could never do.

Habermas distinguishes 'the system' (the fused economic-governmental structure run by instrumental reason) from the 'life world' (where communicative rationality happens); modern media increasingly resembles the salesman, selling values rather than fostering genuine discussion, so the system colonizes the life world -- true democracy would mean the life world controlling the system instead.
